intervals.label: operation
intervals.locator: SLC page on the SLD ALR site (SLAC), first and last paragraphs; SLAC milestones page, 1989 entry
intervals.note: Start at year precision: the SLAC milestones page says "SLC operations begin" in 1989 and the SLC page on the SLD site dates the physics program with the Mark II detector to 1989, but the SLAC handbook page says "Physics at the SLC started in 1988 with the Mark II detector", so the start year differs by one between official SLAC pages. End: "termination in June of 1998" (SLC page); CERN Courier reports the SLC was shut down just before noon on 8 June 1998 "for what may have been the last time". Operating interval; the terminal event is its end.
intervals.quote: The experimental physics program using the SLC started with the MarkII detector in 1989 ... lack of federal funding for this program led to its termination in June of 1998

intervals.label: completed
intervals.locator: SLC page on the SLD ALR site (SLAC), paragraph on the Z0 event totals
intervals.note: Terminal event: the end of the operating interval above. CERN Courier gives 8 June 1998 as the day of the shutdown but was not certain it was final, so only the month is recorded.
intervals.quote: lack of federal funding for this program led to its termination in June of 1998

name: Stanford Linear Collider
notes: The SLC used the SLAC linac itself as its accelerator, not as an injector ("Starting in 1983, extensive modifications and additions to the existing linac enabled it to simultaneously accelerate and collide 50 GeV electrons and positron bunches on a pulse-to-pulse basis", SLAC handbook page): see accelerator:slac-linac.

beam_energy.locator: SLAC graduate handbook page, "The Linac and the SLAC Linear Collider"; SLAC milestones page, 1989 entry
beam_energy.note: Maximum per-beam energy of the SLC linac, not the energy used for physics: to sit on the Z resonance the collider ran at cms/2 ~ 45.5-45.6 GeV per beam (cms energy ~91 GeV). The SLAC milestones page records "SLC operations begin, 50 GeV electron and positron beams achieved" (1989).
beam_energy.quote: Starting in 1983, extensive modifications and additions to the existing linac enabled it to simultaneously accelerate and collide 50 GeV electrons and positron bunches on a pulse-to-pulse basis.

cms_energy.locator: arXiv:hep-ex/0004026, section on the SLC beams (Ecm measured with energy spectrometers); arXiv PDF p. 4
cms_energy.note: Luminosity-weighted mean e⁺e⁻ centre-of-mass energy measured by the SLD at the SLC: 91.26 ± 0.03 GeV (1996 run) and 91.237 ± 0.029 GeV (1997-98 run, calibrated to the Z mass). The recorded value 91 GeV is these figures rounded to the nearest GeV (approx flag set); the collider ran at the Z resonance.
cms_energy.quote: The luminosity-weighted mean e+ e− center-of-mass energy (Ecm ) was measured with precision energy spectrometers [8] and was found to be 91.26±0.03 GeV for the 1996 run.

summary.plain: A particle collider at SLAC that smashed together beams of electrons and positrons tuned to the mass of the Z boson, letting physicists study that particle's properties with the SLD detector from 1989 to 1998.
summary.technical: Stanford Linear Collider: SLAC's linac accelerated electrons and positrons (up to 50 GeV per beam) around a single-pass arc to collide at the Z resonance (~91 GeV cms, ~45.5 GeV/beam), studied by the SLD detector, 1989-1998.
